pool.label: C1
pool.builds_on: the paper’s indication that DED processing parameters critically influence microstructure, extended by using dynamic laser power modulation to induce repeated rapid cooling cycles.
pool.what_is_new: It proposes using a pulsed laser power modulation strategy during DED—a processing route not explored in the paper—to actively control the solidification dynamics and thus tailor microstructure in a Ti–Ni primary HEA.

fields.hypothesis: A modulated laser power strategy during the DED process will produce a cyclic thermal profile that refines the microstructure, thereby improving elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a Ti–Ni primary HEA.
fields.material_initial_state: A Ti–Ni primary HEA fabricated by standard continuous DED processing, exhibiting a relatively coarse grain structure and larger γ′ precipitates due to a consistent high energy input.
fields.intervention: Implement a pulsed or modulated laser power regime (with controlled cyclic variations) during deposition while maintaining complete melting conditions by slight adjustments in laser power and scanning speed.
fields.conditions: The pulse frequency and duty cycle must be optimized to ensure full melting and re-melting of previously deposited layers without inducing defects. All elemental ratios remain within the 5–35 at% range per element.
fields.structural_mediator: A refined microstructure featuring a higher nucleation rate leading to a finer grain size and a more uniform, smaller distribution of coherent γ′ precipitates.
fields.mechanism: By introducing cyclic heat inputs, the molten pool undergoes repeated rapid thermal cycles. Each cycle promotes an enhanced nucleation rate and limits grain growth, which yields a finer grain structure and precipitate distribution. The refined microstructure increases grain boundary area and effective precipitate pinning, thereby impeding dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding at elevated temperatures.
fields.predicted_outcome: The modulated-laser-processed alloy is expected to exhibit an improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance (on the order of roughly 10–20% improvement), with observable reductions in grain and precipitate sizes relative to the baseline.
fields.baseline: Ti–Ni primary HEA produced by standard continuous laser DED processing at otherwise identical power and scanning conditions.
fields.boundary: The modulation parameters must maintain sufficient energy input to ensure complete melting; otherwise, process instabilities or un-melted regions could form.
fields.uncertainty: The benefits of pulsed deposition in this alloy system are anticipated based on prior rapid solidification principles, but the optimal modulation parameters and precise strength improvements require experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of HEA samples using DED: one with a standard, continuous laser power regime, and one with the optimized pulsed/modulated laser power profile. Compare microstructural features via SEM/EBSD and perform high-temperature tensile and creep testing (e.g., at 800 °C).
measurements: Grain size distribution and precipitate size (via SEM/EBSD)
Elevated-temperature yield and ultimate tensile strengths
Creep life under a fixed load
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modulated-laser-processed samples do not exhibit significant grain refinement (e.g., reduction in average grain size by at least 10%) accompanied by a measurable improvement (≥10–15% increase) in high-temperature mechanical properties, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C2
pool.builds_on: the observation in the paper that defect elimination and hot rolling refine the grain structure to improve ductility, extended here by employing a more severe plastic deformation route at cryogenic temperatures to further enhance high-temperature strength via grain refinement
pool.what_is_new: The proposal utilizes cryogenic rolling as an SPD method to achieve an ultrafine-grained structure in a Ti-Ni primary HEA, which has not been explored before for such alloys, along with rapid annealing to preserve the fine grain structure for high-temperature applications.

fields.hypothesis: Severe plastic deformation (SPD) via cryogenic rolling followed by a rapid annealing treatment will refine the grain structure in a Ti-Ni primary high-entropy alloy, enhancing its elevated-temperature mechanical properties.
fields.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with titanium and nickel as the dominant elements (~30 at% each) and additional elements (e.g., Al, Cr, and Mo) in proportions fulfilling the single-phase criteria, initially processed by conventional rolling to form a homogeneous, coarse-grained microstructure.
fields.intervention: Apply cryogenic rolling with high strain (e.g., 70% deformation) at low temperatures, immediately followed by rapid annealing (at a heating rate of ~15 K/s to target temperatures between 750–850 °C for short durations 30–60 s) to induce a uniform ultrafine-grained structure.
fields.conditions: The alloy should have a nominal composition of Ti≈30 at%, Ni≈30 at%, with the balance being elements like Al, Cr, and Mo each in the range 5–35 at%. The processing must be performed in an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation and in a temperature window where dynamic recrystallization occurs without excessive grain growth.
fields.structural_mediator: The resulting ultrafine-grained microstructure with a high density of high-angle grain boundaries.
fields.mechanism: Cryogenic rolling minimizes dynamic recovery, resulting in high dislocation densities and stored strain energy, while rapid annealing promotes uniform recrystallization leading to an ultrafine-grained structure. Fine grains enhance high-temperature strength via grain-boundary strengthening (Hall-Petch effect) and can delay grain-boundary sliding or creep under service conditions.
fields.predicted_outcome: An improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance (estimated improvement on the order of 10–20%) compared to a sample processed by standard room-temperature rolling without SPD.
fields.baseline: A Ti-Ni primary HEA processed by conventional (room-temperature) rolling and annealing without cryogenic deformation.
fields.boundary: The effectiveness is expected within the operating range up to ~800–900 °C; above that, grain coarsening may occur. The composition must support stable ultrafine grains without phase instability.
fields.uncertainty: Precise quantitative improvement in mechanical properties is uncertain due to potential sensitivities to processing parameters and grain-boundary behavior at high temperature.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples with a Ti-Ni primary composition. Process one set using cryogenic rolling (70% strain) followed by rapid annealing at 820 °C for 40 s, and process the other set using standard room-temperature rolling and the same annealing condition. Characterize the grain sizes using EBSD and perform tensile tests and creep tests at elevated temperatures (e.g., 750 °C).
measurements: Grain size distribution
Yield strength at elevated temperature
Creep rate measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cryogenically processed samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in grain size and improvement in yield strength or creep resistance (≥10% improvement) over the baseline samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C3
pool.builds_on: While the paper identifies that dynamic recrystallization and dislocation annihilation contribute to strain softening, this hypothesis introduces carbide precipitation as a means to impede these processes, leveraging metallurgical principles known from carbon-alloyed systems.
pool.what_is_new: It suggests a novel microalloying strategy—adding a trace of carbon to enable in situ formation of nano-carbides—to improve high-temperature mechanical performance in a Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy, an intervention not previously reported in the study.

fields.hypothesis: Microalloying with a trace amount of carbon (0.5–1 at%) will promote the in situ formation of fine TiC (and/or related Ni–Ti carbide) nanoparticles that impede dislocation motion and grain boundary migration, thus enhancing the elevated-temperature yield strength of a Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy.
fields.material_initial_state: A conventionally cast Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy with a B2-ordered structure and a dendritic microstructure established by vacuum melting.
fields.intervention: During the melting process, introduce a controlled carbon addition of 0.5–1 at% so that upon solidification and subsequent low-temperature annealing, dispersed, nano-scale TiC particles form preferentially at dislocation tangles and grain boundaries.
fields.conditions: High-temperature compressive testing in the 1023–1123 K range.
fields.structural_mediator: A refined microstructure featuring nano-scale, stable carbide particles distributed within the matrix and along grain boundaries, acting as pinning sites for dislocations and restraining dynamic recrystallization.
fields.mechanism: The in situ formed TiC particles, due to their high thermal stability, provide a barrier to dislocation motion by forcing dislocations to bow or bypass the particles (Orowan looping). In addition, their presence along grain boundaries helps to stabilize the microstructure by limiting GB sliding and migration during high-temperature deformation.
fields.predicted_outcome: An improvement in yield strength of roughly 10–15% at high temperatures compared to the untreated alloy, along with a reduced rate of strain softening during deformation.
fields.baseline: The baseline is the Ti–Ni primary HEA without carbon addition, exhibiting the microstructural evolution and yield behavior documented in the paper.
fields.boundary: The carbon content must be controlled between 0.5 and 1 at% to ensure the formation of fine, discrete carbides without triggering a continuous carbide network that could embrittle the alloy; the processing and heat treatment temperatures must be compatible with carbide stability.
fields.uncertainty: Thermodynamic predictions for carbide formation in a multi-principal element system are challenging, so the precise morphology and volume fraction of carbides formed are uncertain until experimentally validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two alloy batches: one standard Ti–Ni primary HEA and one with the 0.5–1 at% carbon addition. After identical casting and a controlled post-cast annealing treatment, perform high-temperature (1023–1123 K) compression tests and use TEM/EBSD to verify the formation, distribution, and morphology of TiC nanoparticles.
measurements: Yield strength and corresponding high-temperature stress–strain curves
Microstructural characterization to quantify carbide size, distribution, and volume fraction via TEM/EDS
Fractography to ensure ductility is not adversely affected
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-added alloy does not exhibit at least a 10% improvement in yield strength and microstructural analysis fails to confirm a fine, well-distributed population of TiC nanoparticles compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C4
pool.builds_on: the principle from PMC6170471 that a refined, homogeneous precursor state can enhance spinodal decomposition to yield coherent nanoprecipitates; here extended by using rapid solidification to pre-refine the microstructure in a Ti–Ni primary HEA.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces rapid solidification as a novel processing route for Ti–Ni primary HEAs to pre-establish an ultrafine, homogeneous microstructure that tailors the subsequent spinodal decomposition kinetics and promotes a superior distribution of strengthening nanoprecipitates.

fields.hypothesis: Utilizing rapid solidification processing to produce an ultrafine-grained Ti–Ni primary HEA precursor will create a more homogeneous and refined supersaturated state, thereby enhancing spinodal decomposition kinetics during aging and resulting in a finer, more uniformly dispersed population of coherent nanoprecipitates at elevated temperatures.
fields.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy consisting primarily of titanium and nickel along with at least three additional elements in near-equiatomic proportions, initially prepared via conventional casting to yield a coarse-grained, homogeneous single-phase structure.
fields.intervention: Employ rapid solidification methods (e.g., melt spinning or gas atomization) during alloy fabrication to dramatically increase the cooling rate, yielding an ultrafine-grained structure with suppressed elemental segregation and enhanced supersaturation.
fields.conditions: The rapid solidification process must yield an ultrafine microstructure without altering the overall composition (elements remain within 5–35 at%). Subsequent thermo-mechanical processing (solution treatment, cold working, and aging at ~600 °C for 1 hour) will then be applied to activate spinodal decomposition.
fields.structural_mediator: An ultrafine-grained matrix that, after standard thermomechanical processing, develops a high density of coherent nanoprecipitates (e.g., Ni3Al-type L12 phases or analogous ordering) uniformly distributed throughout the near-equiatomic matrix.
fields.mechanism: Rapid solidification introduces a very fine grain structure and a high degree of supersaturation by quenching in a more homogeneous state. This refined precursor state accelerates the nucleation of spinodal decomposition during subsequent aging, resulting in a significantly refined and uniform dispersion of coherent nanoprecipitates. These nanoprecipitates, with their low lattice misfit and diffuse interfaces, more effectively obstruct dislocation motion at elevated temperatures.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to a conventionally cast alloy, the rapid-solidified and aged alloy is expected to exhibit improved elevated-temperature yield and ultimate tensile strengths – potentially a 15–25% increase – with a finer precipitate size (e.g., reduced by 20–30%) and enhanced uniformity.
fields.baseline: A Ti–Ni primary HEA processed from conventionally cast precursor material and subjected to the same solution treatment, cold rolling, and aging at ~600 °C for 1 hour.
fields.boundary: The rapid solidification processing parameters must be optimized to avoid amorphization or undesirable phases; the final composition and processing route must remain within the HEA definitions.
fields.uncertainty: While rapid solidification has been broadly shown to refine microstructures in alloys, the exact degree to which it enhances spinodal decomposition in a Ti–Ni primary HEA is moderately uncertain and may depend on processing nuances.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the Ti–Ni primary HEA: one via conventional casting and one via rapid solidification (using melt spinning or gas atomization). Subject both to identical solution treatment, cold rolling, and aging at 600 °C for 1 hour. Characterize grain size and precipitate distribution using TEM/EBSD and perform elevated-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: Grain size distribution (via EBSD)
Size, volume fraction, and dispersion uniformity of coherent nanoprecipitates (via TEM/APT)
Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility at high temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapid-solidified alloy does not show a statistically significant refinement in grain size and precipitate morphology, with a corresponding improvement (at least 10–15% increase) in high-temperature mechanical properties compared to the conventional alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C5
pool.builds_on: The paper’s findings that homogeneously distributed sigma precipitates in a BCC matrix enhance elevated-temperature strength, extended here by employing dislocation-enhanced heterogeneous nucleation.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a thermomechanical processing approach (controlled cold deformation prior to heat treatment) in a Ti–Ni primary HEA to refine precipitate dispersion—a processing strategy not explored in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Introducing a moderate cold-deformation step prior to the standard heat treatment will refine the sigma-phase precipitate dispersion in the titanium–nickel primary HEA, thereby enhancing its elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance.
fields.material_initial_state: A titanium–nickel primary high-entropy alloy composed of at least five elements (with Ti and Ni as the primary constituents and other elements such as Al, Nb, and V between 5–35 at% each) processed by conventional casting into a homogeneous single-phase BCC solid solution.
fields.intervention: Apply a moderate cold-working (e.g., 20% thickness reduction via rolling) to introduce a uniform high density of dislocations, followed by the standard homogenization heat treatment at 1100 °C for 1 hour (as used in the baseline study) and subsequent water quenching.
fields.conditions: The cold deformation must be controlled to achieve about 20% reduction without inducing macroscopic cracking. The heat treatment is carried out at 1100°C for 1 hour in a vacuum-sealed environment to prevent oxidation, keeping all elemental concentrations within the 5–35 at% range.
fields.structural_mediator: An increased dislocation density that acts as heterogeneous nucleation sites, leading to a refined and more homogeneously distributed sigma-phase precipitate population within the BCC matrix.
fields.mechanism: Cold deformation introduces numerous dislocations that lower the nucleation barrier for sigma-phase precipitates during subsequent heat treatment. A finer precipitate distribution more effectively obstructs dislocation motion at elevated temperatures, thereby increasing yield strength and improving creep resistance.
fields.predicted_outcome: The thermomechanically processed alloy is anticipated to display an improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength, perhaps on the order of 10–20%, compared to an identical alloy processed solely by conventional casting and heat treatment.
fields.baseline: A titanium–nickel primary HEA produced by conventional casting and a single homogenization heat treatment at 1100 °C for 1 hour without any prior deformation.
fields.boundary: Cold work must be limited (around 20% reduction) to avoid excessive damage or adverse texture development; the heat treatment window (1100 °C for 1 hour) should be strictly maintained to retain the sigma-phase formation kinetics observed in the baseline study.
fields.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement depends on the interplay between dislocation density and precipitate nucleation kinetics, and excessive deformation may lead to defect clustering that undermines properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Ti–Ni primary HEA samples with identical composition. Process one set using conventional casting and heat treatment (1100 °C for 1 h) and the other with a 20% cold-rolling pre-treatment followed by the same heat treatment. Conduct elevated-temperature compressive (or creep) tests at 700 °C and microstructural characterization using SEM/TEM to analyze precipitate size and distribution.
measurements: Elevated-temperature yield strength and creep rate data
Quantitative analysis (e.g., size distribution and volume fraction) of sigma-phase precipitates via microscopic methods
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cold-worked and heat-treated samples do not exhibit at least a 10% statistically significant improvement in yield strength (or a measurable reduction in creep rate) and do not show a noticeably refined and uniformly distributed sigma-phase precipitate population relative to the conventional samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C6
pool.builds_on: The paper’s demonstration that sigma-phase precipitates contribute to enhanced strength and the known benefits of Mo in increasing thermal stability in high-temperature alloys.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes the novel use of a minor Mo addition in a Ti–Ni primary HEA to modify the sigma-phase chemistry for improved high-temperature performance—a compositional modification not explored in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Introducing a minor addition of molybdenum (Mo) into a titanium–nickel primary HEA will modify the composition of the sigma-phase precipitates to enhance their thermal stability, thereby improving elevated-temperature mechanical properties.
fields.material_initial_state: A titanium–nickel primary high-entropy alloy with five or more elements (including Ti, Ni, and other elements such as Al, Nb, and V each in the range of 5–35 at%) formed as a single-phase BCC solid solution by conventional casting.
fields.intervention: Incorporate approximately 5 at.% molybdenum into the alloy composition (adjusting other elements downward to stay within the high-entropy limits) and then subject the alloy to the standard homogenization heat treatment at 1100 °C for 1 hour with water quenching.
fields.conditions: Mo addition should be limited to about 5 at.% to ensure that each element remains within the 5–35 at% range. The heat treatment at 1100 °C for 1 hour should promote sigma-phase nucleation without excessive coarsening. The overall composition must remain balanced and avoid the formation of deleterious phases.
fields.structural_mediator: A modified sigma-phase precipitate population, wherein Mo partitions into the sigma phase, resulting in a structure with increased thermal stability and a refined, uniformly distributed dispersion within the BCC matrix.
fields.mechanism: Molybdenum is known for its high melting point and strong solid-solution strengthening effects. When added in minor amounts, Mo can substitute into the sigma-phase structure (possibly forming a Mo-containing variant of Al(Nb, M,Ti)2) and increase its thermal stability by lowering diffusion rates. The more stable precipitates better obstruct dislocation motion at elevated temperatures, thus enhancing yield strength.
fields.predicted_outcome: The Mo-doped alloy should exhibit improved retention of yield strength at high temperatures (e.g., an increase of roughly 10–20% at 700–800 °C) and potentially better creep resistance compared to the baseline alloy lacking Mo.
fields.baseline: A titanium–nickel primary HEA with the same base composition (e.g., Al0.8NbTiV or a similar variant) processed by conventional casting and heat treatment at 1100 °C for 1 hour without Mo addition.
fields.boundary: The Mo content must remain at approximately 5 at.% to ensure that the alloy remains within the compositional definition of high-entropy alloys; heat treatment parameters must ensure that the sigma phase remains finely distributed without coarsening.
fields.uncertainty: The exact partitioning behavior of Mo in the sigma phase and the quantitative improvement in yield strength require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of samples: one with the baseline Ti–Ni primary HEA composition and one with an additional 5 at.% Mo (balanced by slight reduction of one or more other elements). Process both using 1100 °C for 1 hour heat treatment with quenching. Conduct elevated-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., compression tests at 700–800 °C) and perform microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM/TEM with EDS) to verify differences in precipitate composition and distribution.
measurements: Yield strength and creep behavior at elevated temperatures
Precipitate chemistry, size, and morphology using microscopic techniques and compositional analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-containing alloy does not show at least a 10% improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength (or an observable enhancement in creep resistance) and if microstructural analysis reveals no beneficial modification in sigma-phase composition or dispersion compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C7
pool.builds_on: The principle from the paper that multi-phase microstructures can enhance high-temperature performance, here extended by employing grain refinement technology combined with a minor alloying addition.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a controlled minor addition of Ta combined with thermomechanical processing—an intervention not addressed in the paper—to achieve a refined grain structure, thus providing an alternative route (grain-boundary strengthening) to improve high-temperature mechanical properties in a Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy.

fields.hypothesis: Thermomechanical processing to refine the grain structure via the introduction of a controlled minor addition of a refractory element (e.g., tantalum) will improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of the Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy.
fields.material_initial_state: An as-cast, equimolar Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy displaying a coarse-grained, near single-phase structure with limited inherent grain-boundary strengthening.
fields.intervention: Introduce a small, controlled amount (e.g., 2–5 at%) of tantalum during alloy preparation, followed by hot-forging and subsequent annealing to achieve a refined and stable ultrafine-grained microstructure.
fields.conditions: The alloy composition should remain within the HEA regime (each principal element between 5–35 at%), and the forging/annealing schedule is optimized to refine grains without causing excessive recrystallization; processing temperatures are set below Tm but high enough to facilitate plastic deformation.
fields.structural_mediator: A refined (submicron) grain structure with stabilized grain boundaries strengthened by residual Ta segregation.
fields.mechanism: Refined grains lead to grain-boundary strengthening (Hall–Petch effect), and the minor Ta addition helps pin grain boundaries, limiting grain growth at high temperatures. This dual mechanism improves yield strength and creep resistance under elevated temperature service.
fields.predicted_outcome: A significant improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance compared to the base Ti–Ni alloy; the relative improvement is expected qualitatively, though its precise magnitude remains uncertain.
fields.baseline: The same Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy without the Ta addition and without thermomechanical grain refinement.
fields.boundary: The Ta addition must be minor to avoid forming deleterious intermetallic compounds, and the processing conditions must prevent excessive grain growth; the intervention is valid only within the range where grain-boundary pinning is effective.
fields.uncertainty: The extent of grain refinement and its quantitative contribution to high-temperature performance need to be established experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two batches of the alloy: one with the minor Ta addition and thermomechanical processing (hot-forged and annealed) and another as a standard as-cast alloy. Characterize grain sizes (using EBSD) and perform high-temperature mechanical testing (creep and tensile tests).
measurements: Average grain size (EBSD)
Yield strength at elevated temperatures
Creep rate under constant load at service temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant grain size refinement and corresponding improvements in high-temperature yield strength or reduced creep rate compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C8
pool.builds_on: The paper’s insights into phase formation in HEAs and the recognition that non-equilibrium processing can lead to beneficial microstructural features, combined with the established advantages of rapid solidification techniques.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis leverages an advanced manufacturing route (SLM) to deliberately engineer a non-equilibrium microstructure in a Ti–Ni primary HEA, an approach not explored in the paper, thereby offering a novel method to enhance high-temperature mechanical properties.

fields.hypothesis: Tailoring the solidification conditions via selective laser melting (SLM) can produce a non-equilibrium, refined microstructure in a Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy that enhances elevated-temperature mechanical properties.
fields.material_initial_state: A Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy conventionally produced with equilibrium microstructures (cast or wrought) characterized by coarse grains and possible formation of equilibrium intermetallic phases.
fields.intervention: Employ selective laser melting with optimized laser scan speeds and energy densities to achieve rapid solidification, resulting in a refined, non-equilibrium microstructure with suppressed deleterious intermetallic phases. A subsequent low-temperature subcritical anneal may be applied to reduce residual stresses without coarsening the microstructure.
fields.conditions: Processing parameters must be tuned such that the cooling rate is sufficiently high (on the order of 10^5–10^6 K/s) to refine the microstructure while avoiding the formation of brittle phases and maintaining the overall equimolar composition. Post-processing annealing should be performed at temperatures well below Tm.
fields.structural_mediator: A heterogeneous microstructure characterized by ultra-fine grains and a reduced volume fraction of coarse, equilibrium intermetallics.
fields.mechanism: Rapid solidification during SLM leads to a finer grain structure and can kinetically suppress the precipitation of equilibrium, potentially brittle, intermetallic phases. The resulting microstructure is expected to enhance dislocation blocking and reduce diffusional creep, thus improving elevated-temperature performance.
fields.predicted_outcome: Improved yield strength and creep resistance at elevated temperatures compared to conventionally processed alloys; the improvement is expected qualitatively, with exact enhancements dependent on processing conditions.
fields.baseline: Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy produced via conventional casting or forging, exhibiting equilibrium microstructure with coarser grains and a higher likelihood of deleterious intermetallic phase formation.
fields.boundary: SLM processing parameters must be controlled precisely to avoid excessive porosity or the formation of unwanted phases; the benefits are expected only if a fine microstructure is retained after any necessary subcritical annealing.
fields.uncertainty: The quantitative relationship between SLM processing parameters, microstructure refinement, and high-temperature mechanical properties remains to be determined through systematic experiments.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of alloy specimens: one using optimized SLM processing with subsequent subcritical annealing, and one using conventional casting. Characterize microstructures (using SEM/EBSD) and perform high-temperature tensile and creep tests.
measurements: Grain size distribution (EBSD)
Phase identification (XRD)
Elevated temperature mechanical properties (tensile strength, creep rate)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SLM-processed samples do not display a significantly refined microstructure along with statistically significant improvements in high-temperature mechanical performance relative to the conventionally processed samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C9
pool.builds_on: the concept from the paper that precipitation strengthening is a potent mechanism in HEAs, extended by integrating grain refinement via rapid solidification to further enhance high-temperature mechanical properties.
pool.what_is_new: It introduces a processing route change—rapid solidification—to create an ultrafine-grained HEA that, upon subsequent aging, achieves a synergistic strengthening effect combining grain boundary and precipitation hardening, a strategy not addressed in the original study.

fields.hypothesis: Adopt a rapid solidification processing route (e.g., melt spinning) in a Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy to achieve an ultrafine-grained microstructure that, upon a subsequent controlled aging treatment, results in a high density of fine, uniformly distributed precipitates, thereby enhancing elevated-temperature mechanical properties.
fields.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a composition around Ti 40, Ni 40, Co 7, Cr 6, and Al 7 (all within the 5–35 at% range) produced by conventional casting and homogenization, exhibiting a coarse grain structure with a standard precipitation response.
fields.intervention: Employ rapid solidification (melt spinning) during alloy production to drastically refine the grain size. Follow this with a standard homogenization heat treatment and an optimized aging treatment (e.g., 750°C for 3 hours) designed to nucleate and grow fine precipitates.
fields.conditions: All elements must adhere to the compositional HEA limits. The rapid solidification process must be optimized (e.g., high cooling rates on the order of 10^5 K/s) to achieve ultrafine grains without compromising alloy homogeneity. Elevated-temperature mechanical tests are conducted from 600 to 800°C.
fields.structural_mediator: An ultrafine-grained matrix with a high density of grain boundaries which, together with a refined distribution of nanoscale precipitates (similar to Ni3Ti or related phases), promotes enhanced dislocation hindrance and grain boundary strengthening.
fields.mechanism: Rapid solidification significantly refines the grain size by suppressing dendritic growth and allows for a higher nucleation rate. The subsequent aging treatment leverages the high number of grain boundaries, which serve as additional nucleation sites for precipitates. This synergistic microstructure (grain refinement plus fine precipitation) enhances strength via both Hall–Petch and precipitation hardening mechanisms, crucial for elevated-temperature performance.
fields.predicted_outcome: An enhancement of yield strength and creep resistance by approximately 15–30% at high temperatures (600–800°C) compared to the conventionally cast and homogenized alloy.
fields.baseline: The same HEA composition produced by conventional casting and homogenization, followed by the standard aging treatment, resulting in a relatively coarse grain structure and less refined precipitate distribution.
fields.boundary: The rapid solidification processing must be capable of achieving ultrafine grains without causing compositional segregation. The aging treatment should be optimized to prevent excessive grain growth while promoting nanoscale precipitate formation.
fields.uncertainty: While the beneficial effects of grain refinement and fine precipitation are well established, the precise balance of processing parameters to achieve the desired microstructure in a complex HEA is not fully predictable, making the exact magnitude of improvement somewhat uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the HEA with composition Ti 40, Ni 40, Co 7, Cr 6, and Al 7: one set produced by conventional casting and homogenization, and the other set produced by rapid solidification (melt spinning) followed by identical homogenization and aging treatments. Use EBSD and TEM to compare grain size and precipitate distribution, and perform high-temperature tensile and creep tests between 600–800°C.
measurements: Grain size and boundary density (EBSD, TEM)
Precipitate size and distribution (TEM, XRD)
Elevated-temperature yield strength (tensile testing)
Creep rate under load at 600–800°C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapidly solidified and aged alloy does not display at least a 15% improvement in yield strength/creep resistance at elevated temperatures, or if the ultrafine grain structure and fine precipitate distribution are not distinctly superior to the conventionally processed alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C10
pool.builds_on: the Mo–Ti study’s detailed correction for interstitial oxygen effects on yield strength, which demonstrates that a controlled amount of oxygen can significantly modify dislocation behavior
pool.what_is_new: It proposes the counterintuitive strategy of intentionally introducing a controlled oxygen content into a Ti–Ni‐primary high‐entropy alloy to harness interstitial strengthening, a method not conventionally applied in such alloys where oxygen is typically minimized.

fields.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled, low-level oxygen content (~0.2 at%) during processing will produce interstitial solid solution strengthening in a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high‐entropy alloy, enhancing its elevated‐temperature yield strength by modifying dislocation core dynamics.
fields.material_initial_state: A Ti–Ni‐primary high‐entropy alloy produced under oxygen‐minimized conditions, resulting in minimal interstitial oxygen levels.
fields.intervention: Intentionally expose the alloy to a controlled oxygen partial pressure during melting and homogenization to achieve a uniform dissolved oxygen content of approximately 0.2 at%.
fields.conditions: Testing under elevated temperatures (600–750 °C) where dislocation-controlled plasticity is operative.
fields.structural_mediator: A uniform distribution of interstitial oxygen atoms within the crystal lattice that subtly distorts the local atomic environment.
fields.mechanism: Interstitial oxygen atoms increase the energy barrier for dislocation motion by interacting with dislocation cores — an effect analogous to that observed and corrected for in Mo–Ti alloys. In this case, a controlled oxygen dosage adds a beneficial solid solution strengthening component that is complementary to the inherent substitutional lattice misfit effects, thereby enhancing yield strength at high temperatures.
fields.predicted_outcome: The oxygen-doped alloy should show an improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance (estimated around a 10–15% enhancement, though precise values are uncertain) relative to an alloy processed to minimize oxygen uptake.
fields.baseline: A titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy produced under strict oxygen minimization with negligible interstitial oxygen levels.
fields.boundary: The oxygen level must be carefully controlled (targeting ~0.2 at%) to avoid deleterious effects such as oxide precipitation or excessive embrittlement; processing conditions must ensure uniform oxygen dissolution.
fields.uncertainty: While the beneficial effect of interstitial oxygen on strengthening is supported by analogous systems, the balance between strength improvement and potential embrittlement at high oxygen levels introduces uncertainty in the net outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set processed in an oxygen-minimized environment (baseline) and one set processed with controlled oxygen exposure to achieve ~0.2 at% dissolved oxygen. Use microprobe or atom probe tomography to verify the oxygen content and distribution. Then, conduct elevated-temperature mechanical tests (such as yield testing and creep tests at 650–750 °C).
measurements: Oxygen content and distribution analysis (e.g., via APT or microprobe)
Elevated-temperature yield strength
Creep rate at the designated test temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant enhancement in yield strength (e.g., improvement less than 5% beyond experimental scatter) or if deleterious oxide formation is detected that undermines mechanical integrity, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C11
pool.builds_on: Observations in the paper regarding macrosegregation effects in alloys with boron additions have been extended by employing a tailored solidification rate to directly influence the nucleation and distribution kinetics of boron-induced phases in a Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis integrates a non-standard, intermediate-rate solidification strategy specifically designed to control the kinetics of boron-related phase formation, rather than using a generic rapid solidification approach. It links the processing parameter (cooling rate) directly to the desired nano-phase distribution, an aspect not addressed in the original work.

fields.hypothesis: Controlled Intermediate-Rate Solidification to Tailor the Kinetics of Boron-Induced Nano-Phase Formation in a Ti–Ni Primary High-Entropy Alloy.
fields.material_initial_state: A Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy produced by conventional arc melting that exhibits coarse grains and significant macrosegregation, leading to nonuniform distribution of boron during conventional solidification.
fields.intervention: Adopt a controlled solidification process with an intermediate cooling rate—faster than conventional arc melting but slower than extreme rapid solidification (e.g., using a calibrated melt extraction or drop-tube technique)—combined with a modest boron addition (≈1–2 at%), to precisely influence the nucleation kinetics of boron-bearing nano-phases.
fields.conditions: Process the alloy under an inert atmosphere with a controlled cooling rate (targeted rate to be determined via preliminary trials, for example, 10^3–10^4 K/s) followed by a short homogenization heat treatment (e.g., 100 h at 1200–1300 °C) to reduce residual segregation while preserving a refined microstructure. Evaluate performance in the 800–1100 °C regime.
fields.structural_mediator: A refined microstructure with uniform grain size and homogeneous distribution of fine, boron-induced nano-precipitates. The specific cooling rate minimizes coarse TiB2 formation and promotes the nucleation of sub-micron boron-containing phases that strengthen the alloy.
fields.mechanism: Conventional rapid solidification can refine grains but may lead to excessive undercooling and uncontrolled boron segregation forming coarse borides. By tuning the cooling rate to an intermediate regime, it is possible to simultaneously suppress macrosegregation and tailor the nucleation kinetics such that boron is incorporated into finely dispersed nano-phases (which might be either a borosilicide or a finely precipitated boride with beneficial morphology). This controlled process enhances the density of obstacles to dislocation motion (via both the refined grain boundaries and the homogeneously dispersed nano-precipitates), thus improving elevated-temperature mechanical properties according to the Hall-Petch relationship and precipitation strengthening mechanisms.
fields.predicted_outcome: The alloy processed under the controlled intermediate cooling rate is expected to demonstrate a finer grain structure and a uniform dispersion of boron-induced nano-phase precipitates, resulting in an improvement in high-temperature yield strength and reduced creep rates (estimated ~10–15% improvement) compared to an identically composed alloy processed by conventional solidification.
fields.baseline: A Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy produced by conventional arc melting that shows coarse grains, noticeable macrosegregation, and an inhomogeneous distribution of boron-induced phases, leading to lower high-temperature mechanical performance.
fields.boundary: The cooling rate must be optimized within an intermediate window (e.g., 10^3–10^4 K/s) since too slow yields coarse structures and too fast leads to non-equilibrium phase formation. The boron content should be maintained at around 1–2 at% to avoid excessive formation of coarse, brittle borides.
fields.uncertainty: The exact relationship between the controlled intermediate cooling rate and the kinetics of boron-induced nano-phase formation in the multicomponent Ti–Ni system is not fully determined and requires experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Ti–Ni primary HEA samples with identical alloy chemistry and ~1–2 at% boron: one set processed by conventional arc melting and one set processed using the controlled intermediate-rate solidification method. Follow both sets with the same homogenization heat treatment. Characterize grain size and precipitate distribution by SEM/EBSD and TEM/EDS, respectively. Perform high-temperature tensile and creep tests within 800–1100 °C.
measurements: Grain size distribution and degree of macrosegregation (SEM/EBSD)
Identification and size distribution of boron-induced nano-phases (TEM/EDS)
High-temperature yield strength and creep properties
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the intermediate-rate solidified samples do not show statistically significant grain refinement, a more uniform precipitate distribution, or if mechanical properties do not improve by at least ~10–15% compared to the conventional samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C12
pool.builds_on: the finding from PMC7513041 that microstructural heterogeneity and formation of additional complex phases deteriorate mechanical properties, suggesting that a microstructure limited to cubic phases is beneficial for wear resistance.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis applies a rapid solidification processing intervention to a titanium–nickel primary HEA to deliberately suppress the formation of unwanted brittle phases and achieve a refined microstructure tailored for high-temperature mechanical performance, an approach not explored in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Rapid solidification via melt spinning can improve the elevated‐temperature mechanical properties of a titanium–nickel primary HEA by suppressing the formation of coarse interdendritic brittle phases.
fields.material_initial_state: A titanium–nickel primary high-entropy alloy with a multiphase microstructure produced by conventional arc-melting and slow cooling that forms coarse bcc (B2) and additional undesirable brittle phases at elevated titanium content.
fields.intervention: Process the alloy via a rapid solidification route (e.g., melt spinning or suction casting) to achieve cooling rates on the order of 10^5 K/s.
fields.conditions: Maintain the nominal composition with Ti and Ni as primary constituents; use high cooling rates during solidification (e.g., melt spinning at ~10^5 K/s) while keeping other processing parameters similar except for the cooling rate.
fields.structural_mediator: A refined microstructure with a predominantly single-phase (or a controlled dual-phase) cubic structure that avoids coarse dendritic segregation and the formation of complex brittle phases.
fields.mechanism: Rapid solidification reduces the time available for element partitioning and undesirable phase transformations. This limits the precipitation of brittle intermetallic or complex phases (such as tetragonal σ or cc phases) and results in a finer, more homogeneous microstructure. Finer grains and a suppressed formation of secondary phases enhance the mechanical integrity and creep resistance at elevated temperatures.
fields.predicted_outcome: Enhanced elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance (by reducing sites for crack initiation) with an approximate improvement in strength/hardness relative to conventionally processed alloys. The wear and ductility under high temperature should also improve, although the exact magnitude is uncertain.
fields.baseline: The same titanium–nickel primary HEA produced by arc-melting with slow cooling found to have multiphase microstructures with coarse grain segregation and brittle precipitates as reported in PMC7513041.
fields.boundary: The intervention is applicable when the cooling rate is sufficiently high (around 10^5 K/s) and does not introduce excessive residual stresses; the alloy composition must remain within the titanium–nickel primary regime.
fields.uncertainty: The quantitative improvement in high-temperature properties is not precisely predictable without experimental validation; potential effects of residual stresses from rapid cooling need to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two samples of the titanium–nickel primary HEA with identical nominal composition: one using conventional arc-melting with slow cooling and one using melt spinning to achieve rapid cooling. Characterize the microstructure via SEM and XRD, then conduct elevated-temperature mechanical tests (creep or high-temperature compression tests).
measurements: Phase fraction and grain size determination using SEM/XRD
Elevated-temperature yield strength and creep rate measurements
Hardness and ductility tests at temperatures relevant to intended application
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapidly solidified sample does not show a statistically significant improvement in high-temperature yield strength/creep resistance (or shows a degraded performance) compared to the conventional sample, or if no substantial refinement of microstructure is observed, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

top3.label: C3
top3.builds_on: While the paper identifies that dynamic recrystallization and dislocation annihilation contribute to strain softening, this hypothesis introduces carbide precipitation as a means to impede these processes, leveraging metallurgical principles known from carbon-alloyed systems.
top3.what_is_new: It suggests a novel microalloying strategy—adding a trace of carbon to enable in situ formation of nano-carbides—to improve high-temperature mechanical performance in a Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy, an intervention not previously reported in the study.

fields.hypothesis: Microalloying with a trace amount of carbon (0.5–1 at%) will promote the in situ formation of fine TiC (and/or related Ni–Ti carbide) nanoparticles that impede dislocation motion and grain boundary migration, thus enhancing the elevated-temperature yield strength of a Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy.
fields.material_initial_state: A conventionally cast Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy with a B2-ordered structure and a dendritic microstructure established by vacuum melting.
fields.intervention: During the melting process, introduce a controlled carbon addition of 0.5–1 at% so that upon solidification and subsequent low-temperature annealing, dispersed, nano-scale TiC particles form preferentially at dislocation tangles and grain boundaries.
fields.conditions: High-temperature compressive testing in the 1023–1123 K range.
fields.structural_mediator: A refined microstructure featuring nano-scale, stable carbide particles distributed within the matrix and along grain boundaries, acting as pinning sites for dislocations and restraining dynamic recrystallization.
fields.mechanism: The in situ formed TiC particles, due to their high thermal stability, provide a barrier to dislocation motion by forcing dislocations to bow or bypass the particles (Orowan looping). In addition, their presence along grain boundaries helps to stabilize the microstructure by limiting GB sliding and migration during high-temperature deformation.
fields.predicted_outcome: An improvement in yield strength of roughly 10–15% at high temperatures compared to the untreated alloy, along with a reduced rate of strain softening during deformation.
fields.baseline: The baseline is the Ti–Ni primary HEA without carbon addition, exhibiting the microstructural evolution and yield behavior documented in the paper.
fields.boundary: The carbon content must be controlled between 0.5 and 1 at% to ensure the formation of fine, discrete carbides without triggering a continuous carbide network that could embrittle the alloy; the processing and heat treatment temperatures must be compatible with carbide stability.
fields.uncertainty: Thermodynamic predictions for carbide formation in a multi-principal element system are challenging, so the precise morphology and volume fraction of carbides formed are uncertain until experimentally validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two alloy batches: one standard Ti–Ni primary HEA and one with the 0.5–1 at% carbon addition. After identical casting and a controlled post-cast annealing treatment, perform high-temperature (1023–1123 K) compression tests and use TEM/EBSD to verify the formation, distribution, and morphology of TiC nanoparticles.
measurements: Yield strength and corresponding high-temperature stress–strain curves
Microstructural characterization to quantify carbide size, distribution, and volume fraction via TEM/EDS
Fractography to ensure ductility is not adversely affected
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-added alloy does not exhibit at least a 10% improvement in yield strength and microstructural analysis fails to confirm a fine, well-distributed population of TiC nanoparticles compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C4
top3.builds_on: the principle from PMC6170471 that a refined, homogeneous precursor state can enhance spinodal decomposition to yield coherent nanoprecipitates; here extended by using rapid solidification to pre-refine the microstructure in a Ti–Ni primary HEA.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces rapid solidification as a novel processing route for Ti–Ni primary HEAs to pre-establish an ultrafine, homogeneous microstructure that tailors the subsequent spinodal decomposition kinetics and promotes a superior distribution of strengthening nanoprecipitates.

fields.hypothesis: Utilizing rapid solidification processing to produce an ultrafine-grained Ti–Ni primary HEA precursor will create a more homogeneous and refined supersaturated state, thereby enhancing spinodal decomposition kinetics during aging and resulting in a finer, more uniformly dispersed population of coherent nanoprecipitates at elevated temperatures.
fields.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy consisting primarily of titanium and nickel along with at least three additional elements in near-equiatomic proportions, initially prepared via conventional casting to yield a coarse-grained, homogeneous single-phase structure.
fields.intervention: Employ rapid solidification methods (e.g., melt spinning or gas atomization) during alloy fabrication to dramatically increase the cooling rate, yielding an ultrafine-grained structure with suppressed elemental segregation and enhanced supersaturation.
fields.conditions: The rapid solidification process must yield an ultrafine microstructure without altering the overall composition (elements remain within 5–35 at%). Subsequent thermo-mechanical processing (solution treatment, cold working, and aging at ~600 °C for 1 hour) will then be applied to activate spinodal decomposition.
fields.structural_mediator: An ultrafine-grained matrix that, after standard thermomechanical processing, develops a high density of coherent nanoprecipitates (e.g., Ni3Al-type L12 phases or analogous ordering) uniformly distributed throughout the near-equiatomic matrix.
fields.mechanism: Rapid solidification introduces a very fine grain structure and a high degree of supersaturation by quenching in a more homogeneous state. This refined precursor state accelerates the nucleation of spinodal decomposition during subsequent aging, resulting in a significantly refined and uniform dispersion of coherent nanoprecipitates. These nanoprecipitates, with their low lattice misfit and diffuse interfaces, more effectively obstruct dislocation motion at elevated temperatures.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to a conventionally cast alloy, the rapid-solidified and aged alloy is expected to exhibit improved elevated-temperature yield and ultimate tensile strengths – potentially a 15–25% increase – with a finer precipitate size (e.g., reduced by 20–30%) and enhanced uniformity.
fields.baseline: A Ti–Ni primary HEA processed from conventionally cast precursor material and subjected to the same solution treatment, cold rolling, and aging at ~600 °C for 1 hour.
fields.boundary: The rapid solidification processing parameters must be optimized to avoid amorphization or undesirable phases; the final composition and processing route must remain within the HEA definitions.
fields.uncertainty: While rapid solidification has been broadly shown to refine microstructures in alloys, the exact degree to which it enhances spinodal decomposition in a Ti–Ni primary HEA is moderately uncertain and may depend on processing nuances.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the Ti–Ni primary HEA: one via conventional casting and one via rapid solidification (using melt spinning or gas atomization). Subject both to identical solution treatment, cold rolling, and aging at 600 °C for 1 hour. Characterize grain size and precipitate distribution using TEM/EBSD and perform elevated-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: Grain size distribution (via EBSD)
Size, volume fraction, and dispersion uniformity of coherent nanoprecipitates (via TEM/APT)
Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility at high temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapid-solidified alloy does not show a statistically significant refinement in grain size and precipitate morphology, with a corresponding improvement (at least 10–15% increase) in high-temperature mechanical properties compared to the conventional alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C9
top3.builds_on: the concept from the paper that precipitation strengthening is a potent mechanism in HEAs, extended by integrating grain refinement via rapid solidification to further enhance high-temperature mechanical properties.
top3.what_is_new: It introduces a processing route change—rapid solidification—to create an ultrafine-grained HEA that, upon subsequent aging, achieves a synergistic strengthening effect combining grain boundary and precipitation hardening, a strategy not addressed in the original study.

fields.hypothesis: Adopt a rapid solidification processing route (e.g., melt spinning) in a Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy to achieve an ultrafine-grained microstructure that, upon a subsequent controlled aging treatment, results in a high density of fine, uniformly distributed precipitates, thereby enhancing elevated-temperature mechanical properties.
fields.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a composition around Ti 40, Ni 40, Co 7, Cr 6, and Al 7 (all within the 5–35 at% range) produced by conventional casting and homogenization, exhibiting a coarse grain structure with a standard precipitation response.
fields.intervention: Employ rapid solidification (melt spinning) during alloy production to drastically refine the grain size. Follow this with a standard homogenization heat treatment and an optimized aging treatment (e.g., 750°C for 3 hours) designed to nucleate and grow fine precipitates.
fields.conditions: All elements must adhere to the compositional HEA limits. The rapid solidification process must be optimized (e.g., high cooling rates on the order of 10^5 K/s) to achieve ultrafine grains without compromising alloy homogeneity. Elevated-temperature mechanical tests are conducted from 600 to 800°C.
fields.structural_mediator: An ultrafine-grained matrix with a high density of grain boundaries which, together with a refined distribution of nanoscale precipitates (similar to Ni3Ti or related phases), promotes enhanced dislocation hindrance and grain boundary strengthening.
fields.mechanism: Rapid solidification significantly refines the grain size by suppressing dendritic growth and allows for a higher nucleation rate. The subsequent aging treatment leverages the high number of grain boundaries, which serve as additional nucleation sites for precipitates. This synergistic microstructure (grain refinement plus fine precipitation) enhances strength via both Hall–Petch and precipitation hardening mechanisms, crucial for elevated-temperature performance.
fields.predicted_outcome: An enhancement of yield strength and creep resistance by approximately 15–30% at high temperatures (600–800°C) compared to the conventionally cast and homogenized alloy.
fields.baseline: The same HEA composition produced by conventional casting and homogenization, followed by the standard aging treatment, resulting in a relatively coarse grain structure and less refined precipitate distribution.
fields.boundary: The rapid solidification processing must be capable of achieving ultrafine grains without causing compositional segregation. The aging treatment should be optimized to prevent excessive grain growth while promoting nanoscale precipitate formation.
fields.uncertainty: While the beneficial effects of grain refinement and fine precipitation are well established, the precise balance of processing parameters to achieve the desired microstructure in a complex HEA is not fully predictable, making the exact magnitude of improvement somewhat uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the HEA with composition Ti 40, Ni 40, Co 7, Cr 6, and Al 7: one set produced by conventional casting and homogenization, and the other set produced by rapid solidification (melt spinning) followed by identical homogenization and aging treatments. Use EBSD and TEM to compare grain size and precipitate distribution, and perform high-temperature tensile and creep tests between 600–800°C.
measurements: Grain size and boundary density (EBSD, TEM)
Precipitate size and distribution (TEM, XRD)
Elevated-temperature yield strength (tensile testing)
Creep rate under load at 600–800°C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapidly solidified and aged alloy does not display at least a 15% improvement in yield strength/creep resistance at elevated temperatures, or if the ultrafine grain structure and fine precipitate distribution are not distinctly superior to the conventionally processed alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.
